stem:
Five days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth she has a headache and flashing lights. Blood pressure was normal through pregnancy and at discharge. It is now 164/106 mmHg, and an hour later 158/102 mmHg. The urine protein:creatinine ratio is 15 mg/mmol. Platelets are 108 x 10^9/L. ALT, LDH and creatinine are normal, and the blood film shows no red-cell fragments. She has not had a seizure.

Which diagnosis fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Migraine with aura, with pain pushing up the pressure
options.explanation: Migraine does not explain new hypertension of 164/106 mmHg or a low platelet count. Headache with visual symptoms after birth is pre-eclampsia until shown otherwise.

options.label: B
options.text: Gestational hypertension, as the protein ratio is under 30
options.explanation: Proteinuria is not required. New hypertension with a platelet count below 150 and neurological symptoms meets the definition of pre-eclampsia, even with a protein:creatinine ratio under 30 mg/mmol.

options.label: C
options.text: Pre-eclampsia, from her platelets and visual symptoms
options.explanation: New hypertension after a normotensive pregnancy, with platelets below 150 x 10^9/L and headache with visual disturbance, is pre-eclampsia. It can first appear in the days after birth, and proteinuria is not needed.

options.label: D
options.text: HELLP syndrome, given thrombocytopenia with a headache
options.explanation: HELLP needs haemolysis and raised liver enzymes as well as low platelets. Her ALT and LDH are normal and the film shows no fragments.

options.label: E
options.text: Eclampsia, as the flashing lights are cortical in origin
options.explanation: Eclampsia is defined by a seizure. Visual symptoms are a severe feature of pre-eclampsia that warn of eclampsia; they are not the diagnosis itself.

context: Pre-eclampsia can first present in the weeks after birth; new hypertension with thrombocytopenia or neurological symptoms meets the definition without proteinuria.
